e-21503.knowledge_point: Finding the Laplace Transform of an Integral
e-21503.problem:
Given that $\mathcal{L}\{\cos(\omega t)\}  = \dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}$ for $s>0,$  find the Laplace transform of

$$
\displaystyle g(t)= \int_{0}^{t} \cos\big(\pi\tau\big) \, \textrm{d}\tau, \quad s>0.
$$
e-21503.worked_solution:
We know that if $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$, then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{\int_{0}^{t} f(\tau) \, \text{d}\tau \right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t) = \cos(\pi t).$ Thus, for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L{f(t)} \\  & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L{{\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi τ)\,\text{d}τ} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
4s

ss−4

1s(s−4)

decision.explanation: The Laplace transform of e^{4t} is 1/(s-4). Integrating from 0 to t divides its transform by s, giving 1/[s(s-4)] for s>4.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Given that $L{{e}^{at}}=\frac{1}{s-a}$ for $s>a$, find the Laplace transform of
$g(t)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{4τ}\,\text{d}τ$
for $s>4.$
after.worked_solution:
We know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)={e}^{4t}.$ Thus, for $s>4,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L{f(t)} \\  & =L{{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s>4,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L{{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{4τ}\,\text{d}τ} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: With ω=2, the Laplace transform of cos(2t) is s/(s²+4). Integration from 0 to t divides the transform by s, giving 1/(s²+4) for s>0.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Given that $L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}$ for $s>0$, find the Laplace transform of
$g(t)={\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2τ)\,\text{d}τ$
for $s>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

In our case, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).$ Thus, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =L{f(t)} \\  & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the integral identity above, we have that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L{{\int }_{0}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2τ)\,\text{d}τ} \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$
